the role of the serotogenic system at the interface between aggression and suicidality is complex and multifactorial, and is still far from being understood.

, although there is no doubt that alterations in 5HT-ergic neurochemistry are implicated in the pathophysiological mechanisms of aggressive and suicidal behaviour, the precise nature of such alterations and their implications for the development of new therapies remain unclear.

5-HT dysfunctions play a major role in the pathogenesis of aggressive and suicidal behaviour, although the nature and extent of this role may vary according to the individual and the specific condition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while 5-HT-ergics may not be the sole determinant of aggressive and suicidal behaviour, they may be the final common pathway for the expression of a number of genetic and environmental factors that contribute to the development of impulsive aggression.
serotonin is a key player in the regulation of impulsive aggression, but its role is more complex than originally anticipated.

5-HT is not the only neurotransmitter involved in the pathophysiological mechanism of aggressive and suicidal behaviour, but it plays a key role in the integration of the neurochemical systems involved.
The main takeaway from our work is that

5-HT-ergics may not represent a single pharmacological target, but rather that the 5-HT system may represent a network of targets that can be manipulated in a selective manner to achieve the desired therapeutic effects, depending on the clinical presentation of the patient.

the role of 5-HT in the regulation of aggressive and suicidal behaviour is complex, and that it is not possible to draw a clear-cut relationship between 5HT and the pathophysiology and/or treatment of these behaviours.

a better understanding of the neurobiological basis of aggressive and suicidal behaviour will provide the necessary framework for the development of new and more effective treatments for these conditions.
